metaDescription: Small vs large marble terrazzo honing volume pricing: $4-$6.50/sq ft under 1,000 sq ft vs $1.75-$3.25 at 25,000+. Compare your stone bids in our comparator.
excerpt: Stone honing unit prices fall sharply as square footage rises because mobilization, minimums, and setup are spread across more floor. Learn where the price breaks happen between a 2,000 sq ft suite entry and a 25,000+ sq ft terrazzo building, and how to capture volume pricing either way.
quickAnswer: Small marble or terrazzo areas under 1,000 sq ft typically pay $4.00-$6.50 per sq ft or simply the $450-$900 job minimum, while 2,000-5,000 sq ft lobbies land around $2.75-$4.50. Buildings with 25,000+ sq ft of terrazzo corridors can negotiate $1.75-$3.25 per sq ft for a hone, polish, and seal because crews run consecutive nights with ride-on or large planetary equipment.

blocks.text: Why Square Footage Changes the Stone Honing Unit Price

Stone restoration has a heavy fixed cost per job. Before a single square foot is honed, the vendor has to load a trailer with a planetary machine, diamond tooling sets, wet vacuums, a squeegee and slurry containment kit, a generator or confirmed 220V access, sealers, and masking supplies. Setup, edge masking, and teardown take roughly two crew-hours regardless of whether the area is 600 or 6,000 sq ft. On a small suite entry, that fixed cost can be 30-50% of the invoice. On a 30,000 sq ft terrazzo floor, it disappears into the rounding.

The second driver is machine size. Small areas are worked with 17-20 inch machines and hand-held edgers. Large open terrazzo halls allow 27-32 inch planetary grinders or ride-on units that cover two to three times as much floor per pass. Crew productivity, not material cost, is what sets most of the unit price.

Small Suite Scenario: 1,800 sq ft Office with a 450 sq ft Marble Entry

A dental or law office with a single marble reception area rarely clears the vendor minimum. A 450 sq ft entry at $4.50 per sq ft would price at $2,025, but if the floor only needs a polish and seal at $2.00, the math says $900, which is right at the top of most minimums. In practice the small office pays the minimum, so the goal becomes adding value inside it.

items: Add restroom marble thresholds, a granite reception counter polish, or a stone window sill run to the same visit at no extra mobilization.
Coordinate with neighboring tenants on the same floor so the vendor can do two or three suites in one night and split the trip.
Ask the landlord whether common-area lobby work is already scheduled and piggyback on that mobilization.
Prioritize daily care: a compact cordless scrubber like the Tennant i-mop Lite, with its 14.5-inch path, can maintain a small stone entry without a full-size machine.

blocks.text: Large Building Scenario: 32,000 sq ft Terrazzo Corridors

A county administration building or older corporate campus with 32,000 sq ft of cement terrazzo corridors is a different procurement exercise. Vendors bid this as a phased project, typically 2,000-2,500 sq ft per night with a three- or four-person crew, which means 13-16 working nights. Because the crew, equipment, and tooling stay on site, the mobilization is charged once, and diamond tooling cost per foot drops.

blocks.text: For buildings this size, the nightly janitorial crew's equipment matters more than at small sites. A 17-inch battery scrubber-dryer like the Clarke Focus II, with a 6 gal tank and 200 RPM disk head, can keep honed terrazzo corridors free of grit between restorations. Pair it with daytime mechanical sweeping at entrances using a quiet sweeper such as the Rubbermaid Commercial 421288 to stop sand from reaching the polished field.

blocks.title: Negotiate repeat-night pricing
blocks.text: On large jobs, ask for a separate unit rate for nights two onward. Vendors often discount 10-15% once tooling is broken in and the crew has dialed in water and slurry handling. Also request a maintenance polish option priced per sq ft so you can lock in lower rates for the following year.
How to Compare Small and Large Stone Bids Fairly

items.name: Normalize to the same scope
items.text: Confirm every bidder quotes the same starting grit, finishing grit, sealer, and number of coats before comparing unit rates.

items.name: Separate fixed from variable cost
items.text: Ask each bidder to break out mobilization so you can see how much of a small job is overhead.

items.name: Check nightly productivity
items.text: Divide total square footage by nights on site; numbers far above 1,200 sq ft per night on a full hone deserve questions.

items.name: Price the phasing
items.text: For large buildings, confirm how corridors stay open, where wet areas are barricaded, and whether ADA routes remain accessible.

items.name: Lock follow-up rates
items.text: Request a per-sq-ft rate for polish-and-seal maintenance visits in years two and three.

faqs.q: Can a small office avoid the job minimum altogether?
faqs.a: Rarely on its own. The realistic options are bundling additional stone surfaces into the same visit, coordinating with neighboring tenants, or asking building management to add your suite to a scheduled common-area restoration. A shared mobilization can bring the effective cost of a 450 sq ft entry down by a third or more.

faqs.q: Do large buildings need a different contract structure?
faqs.a: Yes. Large terrazzo jobs should be written as a project agreement with a phasing plan, daily square-foot targets, a certificate of insurance naming the owner and manager as additional insureds, and retainage released after a final walk-through. Many owners hold back 5-10% until a 30-day touch-up period ends.

faqs.q: Does volume pricing apply to seal-only visits?
faqs.a: It does, but the spread is narrower. Seal-only work is fast, often 3,000-5,000 sq ft per night, so small jobs still hit the minimum while large buildings drop from roughly $1.25 to $0.45 per sq ft. Because the labor is light, mobilization dominates the small-site invoice.

faqs.q: How do safety rules differ between small and large stone jobs?
faqs.a: The rules are the same, but exposure grows with scale. Wet grinding controls silica dust better than dry methods, which matters under OSHA's respirable crystalline silica standard on cement terrazzo. Larger jobs also need wet-floor barricades along long corridors, SDS binders for sealers under HazCom, and lockout procedures if machines run on temporary 220V circuits.

faqs.q: Should the janitorial contractor handle polishing on large floors?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most janitorial vendors are not tooled for diamond honing and would subcontract it with a markup of 10-25%. For large floors, contracting a stone specialist directly and keeping the janitorial scope to daily dust mopping and neutral auto-scrubbing typically yields better pricing and clearer accountability.
